newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris trial Monday for Moslem fundamentalists.
newsitem.headline: Paris trial Monday for Moslem fundamentalists.

text.p: The trial opens on Monday of 34 Moslem fundamentalists accused of backing a Moroccan guerilla group amid fears the case could prompt further attacks like that which killed three people on a Paris commuter train last week.

No formal link has been established between the two cases. But several anonymous telephone calls to newspapers and radios after Tuesday's bombing said there would be further attacks if France did not release Moslem fundamentalists held in its jails. None of the calls is known to have been authenticated.

No one has claimed responsibility for Tuesday's blast, in which 94 people were injured, but French newspapers said a list of suspects Paris sent to other European countries was thought to be composed solely of Islamic activists.
Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed responsibility for an earlier wave of bomb attacks in France in 1995 in which eight people were killed and 160 injured.
The men who go on trial in Paris on Monday are among nearly 200 fundamentalists detained after the 1995 attacks.

Those going on trial are nearly all French Moslems in their mid and late 20s, children of Algerian or Moroccan immigrants recruited in run-down, high-rise suburbs near Paris, Orleans and the eastern town of Besancon which all have large Arab minorities.
They were recruited by Morocco's outlawed Islamic Youth Movement whose aim was to overthrow King Hassan and create an Islamic regime in the North African country, prosecutors say.
But the group also had support from Algerian fundamentalists and one man on trial, Djamel Lounici, is accused of membership of the armed wing of the Algerian Islamic Salvation front (FIS).
Members of the group were recruited in France and sent for weapons training aboard, including to Afganistan. They carried out hold-ups in France to finance their activities, prosecutors say.
Those recruits sent to Morocco shot dead two Spanish tourists during an attack on a hotel in Marrakesh in 1994 while others engaged in a gunfight with police in Fez.

But most of their missions were either botched, like an attack in which Moroccan Jews were to be targetted and where a Casablanca cemetery wall was machine-gunned, or not carried out at all like an intended attack against a Tangiers beach filled with tourists.
Three members of the group, including two French passport holders, are now awaiting execution in Morocco while three others, including one Frenchman, were sentenced to life terms there.
Only 21 of the 34 accused will be in the dock in Paris. The others are being sought by authorities.

Little new information was available about the investigation into Tuesday's attack. Newspapers say investigators believe the bomb weighed up to 20 kg (44 lbs) and was packed in a bulky gas canister placed under a seat in a wheeled bag similar to those used by grocery shoppers.
Police were also investigating the theft last month from a petrol station in an Algerian immigrant area of around 40 gas canisters of the type used in the attack, newspapers said.
